reading.title: How Ecologists Map a Recovering River
reading.purpose: Follow the thinking steps scientists use to combine field data into a clear river report.
paras: When a town removes an old concrete dam, ecologists arrive with nets, notebooks, and water sensors. Their first job is to delineate the study zone, marking the exact upstream and downstream edges where measurements will happen. Before collecting a single sample, the team may postulate that cleaner gravel beds will help native fish return, treating that starting assumption as something to test rather than accept on faith.

Next, researchers hypothesize specific outcomes they can check in the field. For example, they predict that dissolved oxygen will rise within six months as faster currents churn the water. To avoid jumping to conclusions, they contextualize every reading by recording rainfall, air temperature, and nearby farm runoff. Without that setting, a sudden dip in water clarity could be misread.

One sensor alone is never enough. Scientists corroborate their stream gauges by checking independent data from insect counts and satellite images. They also juxtapose photographs taken before and after dam removal, placing the two views side by side so shifts in sandbars and shade trees jump out at once. A single returning species, such as river trout, can exemplify the wider recovery of the entire food web.

At the end of the year, the lead biologist must synthesize months of charts, photos, and lab notes into one unified report. Using five seasons of steady growth, the team can carefully extrapolate how fish numbers might climb over the next decade. Finally, they articulate their findings in plain language at a town meeting so residents can see how scientific thinking turns raw clues into wise local choices.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "juxtapose" most nearly means
choices: to hide old photographs until a study is completely finished
to place two things side by side so differences stand out
to guess how many fish will live in a river ten years later
to remove an old concrete dam from a fast-moving stream
qs.why: Paragraph 3 defines juxtapose directly as "placing the two views side by side so shifts in sandbars and shade trees jump out at once."

qs.q: Which sentence shows why scientists record weather and farm runoff alongside river readings?
choices: Next, researchers hypothesize specific outcomes they can check in the field.
For example, they predict that dissolved oxygen will rise within six months as faster currents churn the water.
To avoid jumping to conclusions, they contextualize every reading by recording rainfall, air temperature, and nearby farm runoff.
Without that setting, a sudden dip in water clarity could be misread.
qs.why: This sentence explains the exact risk of skipping context: a sudden dip in water clarity could be misunderstood.

ev.text: Without that setting, a sudden dip in water clarity could be misread.

qs.q: How do scientists corroborate the data from their stream gauges?
choices: By comparing them with separate evidence from insect counts and satellite images.
By asking residents at a town meeting which fish they prefer to catch.
By deleting any measurements collected during weeks with heavy rainfall.
By replacing every water sensor with a new model every six months.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 states that scientists corroborate stream gauges "by checking independent data from insect counts and satellite images."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Removing concrete dams is always the cheapest way to bring trout back to a town.
Satellite photos are far more accurate than stream gauges or field notebooks.
Ecologists follow disciplined steps—from testing to combining evidence—to explain river recovery.
Town meetings usually slow down scientists who want to publish their annual reports.
qs.why: The reading traces how ecologists delineate, hypothesize, contextualize, corroborate, synthesize, extrapolate, and articulate findings.

clues.text: marking the exact upstream and downstream edges
checking independent data from insect counts and satellite images
placing the two views side by side
months of charts, photos, and lab notes into one unified report
